title: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
description: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosisByMaia Davies and Sarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentRe
body: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosisByMaia Davies and Sarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromRomePope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery."After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.Figure caption, Pope Leo announced on Sunday that he would undergo surgery to remove a growth on his lungWhat is lung adenocarcinoma?Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

schema.headline: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say

title: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
description: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside,
body: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000)."Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a  shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day."Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here."I really like it here."

schema.headline: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird

title: Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim
description: Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the D
body: Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo.The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says.The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant"."Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said."Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added.The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit."Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said.The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death.It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities.He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings.Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

schema.headline: Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim

title: Republic of Ireland: Public sector strike begins
description: Hundreds of thousands of workers on strike across Republic of IrelandImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The strike action will last 24 hoursByAdam M
body: Hundreds of thousands of workers on strike across Republic of IrelandImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The strike action will last 24 hoursByAdam MandevilleBBC News NIMore than 300,000 workers, including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, are on strike across the Republic of Ireland.It comes amid an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government, with a further strike planned on 21 October. It is expected schools could be closed with hospital appointments cancelled and picket lines formed across the country during the 24-hour strike.At the end of September, more than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures.At the start of October, primary and secondary school teachers in the Republic began work-to-rule action.Previously almost 97% of Fórsa members, who voted in an industrial ballot, did so in favour of action. It is the Republic's biggest public service union.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Strike action is taking place across the Republic of IrelandBrendan O'Brien divisional organiser of SIPTU, which represents public sector health and administration workers, previously said the "goodwill" of workers was a large part of what kept public services going.However, he said the Irish government's failure to establish a basis for formal talks "left our members with no alternative but to act collectively".On Tuesday Jack Chambers, the Republic's minister for expenditure, described the strike action as "deeply disappointing" saying it would cause significant disruption to the economy, with thousands of hospital appointments set to be cancelled and schools closed.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Public sector workers outside Leinster House in DublinDawn Hutchings-Walsh is a teacher at Hartstown Community School in Dublin, and commutes from County Wicklow every day.Speaking to Irish broadcaster RTÉ she said the "pay just isn't stretching the way that it used to".Her colleague Sinéad McCarthy said she had to take a career break and move to Dubai for a couple of years to save money for a deposit."It's just not feasible in Ireland to be able to save for a house considering the circumstances and the money that we are on here in this country," she said.Linda Kelly is the general secretary of the Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) said teachers are "really struggling in terms of their pay"."They don't feel like the government is taking them seriously, there's a lot of disappointment with the laissez-faire approach from government over the last couple of months."There's been ample time to solve this issue and the government has sat on its hands and this is the result now," Kelly told RTÉ.

schema.headline: Republic of Ireland: Public sector strike begins

title: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds
description: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connecte
body: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said."Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".The US government has not commented.In the early hours of Thursday, Russian strikes killed two people in the Dnipropetrovsk region, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities. Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.Late on Wednesday, Musk wrote on X, responding to a post saying that Zelensky would not end the war until Russia was defeated, "And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go". He has made similar comments before.Earlier this week he said said: "I agree, time for Ukraine to get a new leader," after Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 the country has been under martial law, meaning elections have been suspended.

schema.headline: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds

title: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel livestream execution
description: A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an
body: A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an execution by firing squad."We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," they wrote in a letter where they also argued the livestream would turn the mass killer into a "martyr".Last week, the Pentagon announced it would publicly show the 3 December execution of Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base.Lawmakers from both parties, as well as religious leaders, have criticised the plan.Last week President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but some administration officials are now leaning against it, according to CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. CBS reported that Trump had not yet made a final decision on the livestream as of Tuesday.In the open letter released on Wednesday, the former military leaders - which included 45 generals, 12 admirals and several former judge advocates general - said they did not oppose the death penalty being carried out.But they argued a public execution would violate the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment and turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into "a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators"."This type of exploitative broadcasting  - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," they also wrote. "It will be used by our nation's enemies to stoke hatred, harm American soldiers and citizens in the future, and will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers."The letter's signatories came from throughout the military and included a handful of officers who retired during Trump's first term. Some also had served during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars.Hasan said in court that he carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American base, believing he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.Retired Maj Gen Tony Taguba, who led the Army's investigation into reported prisoner abuses at Abu Ghraib in Iraq, and retired Air Force Coll Moe Davis, a prosecutor at the Guatanamo Bay detention centre who called waterboarding torture, signed the letter. So did Charles Bolden, a US Marine Corps Major General who became the head  of Nasa, and retired Lt Gen Claudia Kennedy, the first woman to become a three-star general in the Army.

schema.headline: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel livestream execution

title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
description: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly
body: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau."Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

schema.headline: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022

title: Sally Rooney books including Normal People and Intermezzo withdrawn from sale in UK over author's Palestine Action support
description: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Act
body: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books to UK retailers."I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.Normal People was published in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work."To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage.The group's activities have included targeting arms companies linked to Israel's war in Gaza.In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: "In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. "The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland."In her article last August in the Irish Times, Rooney said she would continue using proceeds from her work to support the group despite that being an offence in the UK, and cancelled a UK trip to pick up an award over fears she would be arrested.In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney continued: "As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence."After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK."Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said Rooney had taken "a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced".Ammori said the author's work being withdrawn marked "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action".More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of Palestine Action.About 2,500 have been charged, although none have gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription continues and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month.

schema.headline: Sally Rooney books including Normal People and Intermezzo withdrawn from sale in UK over author's Palestine Action support

title: South East Asia haze: What's choking Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia?
description: Who's to blame for the toxic haze choking South East Asia?  Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian
body: Who's to blame for the toxic haze choking South East Asia?  Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offendersByKoh EweReporting fromSingaporeAs Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra has turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.The smog - or haze - has drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland, as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño: a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.Slash and burnMany of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops. But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy over the haze.Figure caption, Watch: What makes fires in Indonesia so hard to extinguish?A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implements robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished."We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze. The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.Also in 2015,  Indonesia's then-vice-president Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads the Indonesian government's communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests"."When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.But in the past Indonesia has also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze. This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires, though Jakarta has not officially requested international support.Figure caption, Watch: Toxic smog makes thousands sick as Indonesia wildfires rageIn Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society groups to force the government to take action.In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the covering healthcare costs.A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra but was dismissed.Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have been at dangerous levels for weeks.There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day."I'm short of breath and have a headache from breathing this air. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week."The government must also think about common people like us. Please take action to find a solution so that this haze problem can be resolved immediately."

schema.headline: South East Asia haze: What's choking Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia?

title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
description: Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)ByLaura CressTechnology reporterA
body: Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)ByLaura CressTechnology reporterA Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings. But, here's we do know so far.Help from a chatbotThe engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.Hiding in plain toilet paperOn 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper. A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been insertedWho is Abdulrahman Alfozan?Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream."These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt." On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.The FBI investigation is ongoing.If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

schema.headline: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer

title: Australia’s first Michelin stars awarded to 11 restaurants
description: Australia's first-ever Michelin stars go to 11 restaurants in one stateImage source, Supplied: Magill Estate RestaurantImage caption, Magill Estate Re
body: Australia's first-ever Michelin stars go to 11 restaurants in one stateImage source, Supplied: Magill Estate RestaurantImage caption, Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide, whose menu is pictured here, received two Michelin starsByFlorence FreemanAustralia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each.South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country.Magill chef and owner Scott Huggins said he had "dreamt of working in Michelin star restaurants as a youngster".He said he had worked in Michelin star restaurants in Europe and Japan."It's one thing working for one, one thing achieving two [Michelin stars]," he said.Image source, Supplied: Michelin GuideImage caption, Scott Huggins, of Magill Estate Restaurant, receives his two star award Wednesday's announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia.Michelin has approached the national tourism board about bringing the guide to the country more than once, with no luck.South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News."It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said.The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion.Created by brothers André and Édouard Michelin in 1900, the guide was originally designed to encourage motorists to travel - ultimately boosting their core business of selling tyres. It offered drivers maps and recommendations for places to eat and stay, before evolving into one of the best-known names in restaurant recognition.Michelin stars were introduced in 1926 and have since become a major distinction for chefs and restaurants around the world.One star recognises high-quality cooking, two stars indicate excellent cooking worth a detour, while three stars are reserved for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey.Among the one-star recipients is Arkhé in Norwood, which specialises in open-fire cooking, while Aptos in Adelaide serves a tasting menu focused on native Australian ingredients. Here is the full list:Two Michelin starsMagill Estate Restaurant, Rosslyn ParkOne Michelin starAnvers Restaurant, KangarillaMaxwell Restaurant, McLaren ValeBotanic, AdelaideArkhé, NorwoodEsmay, AdelaideAurora at ILA, AdelaideHentley Farm, SeppeltsfieldLVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand, WoodsideAptos, StirlingSkillogalee Barrel House, SevenhillThe wider guide includes more than 70 other South Australian restaurants, with some recognised through the Bib Gourmand category, which highlights restaurants offering good food at more moderate prices.

schema.headline: Australia’s first Michelin stars awarded to 11 restaurants

title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says
description: Image source, Social Media/via REUTERSImage caption, Video posted on social media showed containers floating off the coast of Oman's Musandam peninsul
body: Image source, Social Media/via REUTERSImage caption, Video posted on social media showed containers floating off the coast of Oman's Musandam peninsulaByDavid GrittenA Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.Image source, AFPImage caption, The China-flagged container shipping vessel Hui Fa off Khor Fakkan, in the Gulf of Oman, on TuesdayThe Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

schema.headline: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says

title: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
description: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air f
body: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.US President Donald Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and  Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?

title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
description: A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dra
body: A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history.Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed.The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed.He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth.He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, but a court spokeswoman said he had now waived his anonymity.Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure. The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts. "[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!"In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock. They said later that  "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction, external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".In August 2025, Kuznetsov was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, when his surname emerged in court documents, Kuznetsov was transferred to Germany late last year.German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

schema.headline: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines

title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
description: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.Vehicle fuel prices jumped by
body: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

schema.headline: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
